newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem criticized for defending Argentine tycoon.
newsitem.headline: Menem criticized for defending Argentine tycoon.

text.p: Former Argentine Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo criticised President Carlos Menem on Wednesday for standing up for a businessman who has been linked to the murder of news photographer Jose Luis Cabezas.

Cavallo, who calls postal tycoon Alfredo Yabran a mafia "godfather" with powerful contacts in government, criticised Menem for saying on Tuesday that those who link Yabran with the crime "want to damage the the government's image."

Menem accused the media of "condemning" Yabran and told them "everyone is innocent until the contrary is proved." He made the statement the same day police psychiatrists provided the strongest link yet between Yabran and the murder of the Noticias magazine photographer in January.
Menem's defence fuelled speculation that he and Yabran, who says he is worth $400 million, are friends -- something Menem denies but others such as his ex-wife Zulema Yoma say is true.

"I am surprised at the president saying that at this stage of events because I think those who provide information are trying to clear up this terrible crime and not let it go unpunished," Cavallo told reporters.

The 35-year-old newsman was beaten, handcuffed, shot and his body burned. The murder, which recalled the methods of the death squads of the late 1970s, has sparked mass protests and has influenced the political debate ahead of congressional elections in October and the presidential race in 1999.
The Yabran connection has also begun to worry the business world, where one bond dealer said: "This Yabran business is worrying the market because he has links with government."

Cavallo accuses Menem, Cabinet ministers and judges of protecting Yabran, a friend of Menem's brother-in-law who is accused by the media of secret contacts with senior officials to get Yabran off the hook in the Cabezas case.

Yabran, who has given evidence but not been charged, has been questioned about phone calls to his house in the days before the murder by ex-policeman Gustavo Prellezo, who is accused of having Cabezas abducted and of pulling the trigger.
Two psychiatrists testified that Prellezo told them he had been instructed to "give Mr. Cabezas a fright, not to kill him. That's what was agreed and discussed with Mr. Yabran."

Prellezo's lawyer denied any such confession on Wednesday and prominent opposition Radical Party politician Cesar Jaroslavsky told local radio that his friend Yabran "has no responsibility at all for this horrible murder."

Yabran is suing Cavallo for accusing him of being a "mafia" boss and has paid for advertisements in national newspapers complaining of persecution. He said his accusers were trying to further their political careers or remove him from competition in upcoming privatisations of the state post office and the airports.
